title: NexusPay - POC scoping: workload & benchmark planning
summary: POC scoping call to define success criteria, traffic model (QPS, concurrency), input/output token distributions and benchmark plan. Redwood AE + SE walked NexusPay stakeholders through typical workload profiling, recommended benchmark tests (latency p50/p95/p99, throughput at target QPS, token cost per 1M), and proposed 4-week POC timeline with staged benchmarks. Customer requested VPC deployment options, SOC2 docs, and a performance run with 50K monthly active users simulated (peak 200 QPS). Next steps: Redwood to share benchmark plan & pricing sheet, NexusPay to provide sample traffic traces and sample prompts, schedule benchmark run week of Sep 6.
next_steps: Redwood: send POC benchmark plan + test harness instructions by 2027-08-27
NexusPay: share 7 days of anonymized traffic traces and 200 sample prompts by 2027-08-30
Schedule live benchmark run week of 2027-09-06 (Redwood/Liam to coordinate)
Redwood: provide SOC2 and security pack link by 2027-08-26
Redwood: draft POC SOW and email pricing for 4-week pilot by 2027-08-28

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-08-25
Time: 14:00 PT
Duration: 55 min
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Patel (Redwood SE), Rajiv Malhotra (Head of ML - NexusPay), Sofia Torres (CTO - NexusPay), Ethan Cole (SRE - NexusPay)
 
Auto-summary: (auto) Discussed POC scope, workload characterization, target QPS/concurrency, token size distributions, success criteria, and benchmark plan. Agreed on 4-week POC with staged runs.

Transcript:
00:00 Maya Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, quick intro i'm maya from redwood inference, will keep this tight, liam our se is here to dig into perf.
00:08 Sofia Torres: thanks maya, hi all, we want to validate costs and latency for our payments assistant use case, thinking about a short pilot.
00:15 Rajiv Malhotra: yeah current stack is a mix of open models hosted on cloud VMs and a small amount of openai for chat, but cost is creeping up. looking to see if we can get predictable latency at scale and lower unit cost.
00:28 Liam Patel: cool, that helps. quick q  —  what are your current peak qps and concurrency numbers? approximate is fine.
00:34 Rajiv Malhotra: so peak for the last month, about 180 rps at busiest minute, sustained about 60 qps over business hours, concurrency varies cause of websocket sessions but roughly 80 concurrent sessions during peaks.
00:47 Maya Chen: great, so peak ~180 qps, sustained 60, concurrency ~80. for the pilot we usually model a few scenarios: baseline latency target, cost target, and failure modes. what latency SLO do you have for the assistant?
01:02 Sofia Torres: users expect sub-1s for short lookups, but for longer generative flows 2-3s is acceptable. our internal target is p95 < 1.2s for simple prompts.
01:15 Liam Patel: okay that's helpful, do you have average token sizes for inputs and outputs? like distribution?
01:21 Rajiv Malhotra: average input around 60 tokens, outputs avg 120 tokens, but there's a long tail  —  some batch jobs produce 800-1k tokens. most interactive flows are 40-200 output tokens.
01:35 Maya Chen: perfect, tail noted. for workload modeling we'll use a mixed distribution: 70% short (input 20-80 / output 40-150), 25% medium (input 80-200 / output 200-600), 5% long (input >200 / output >600). does that align?
01:51 Rajiv Malhotra: yeah that's a fair split. also note about 10% of traffic is embeddings for search which is much shorter tokens but higher qps bursts during indexing.
02:05 Liam Patel: good flag  —  we'll include an embeddings workload in the benchmark. next, what's your acceptance criteria for the POC? is it purely latency/cost or also quality?
02:14 Sofia Torres: it's triaged  —  1) latency and throughput must meet p95/p99 targets, 2) unit cost per 1M tokens should be below our current baseline by at least 20%, and 3) no major regressions in output quality as measured by a small eval set (we'll provide prompts).
02:31 Maya Chen: good  —  we'll run baseline comparisons against your current model (if you provide logs) and against an anchored open model. we'll also log p50/p95/p99 and tokenized cost for the run.
02:43 Rajiv Malhotra: one operational question  —  can you run private deployment? we have PCI-sensitive flows, so VPC or private cluster is preferable.
02:52 Liam Patel: yes, Redwood supports private (VPC + on-prem options). for the POC we can do a VPC peering test and run a dedicated capacity pilot; that said, hosted env with encrypted logs is faster to stand up if you want an initial proof.
03:06 Ethan Cole: if we do VPC peering, need to review IP ranges, KMS integration for keys, and audit logs retention. we also need SOC2 docs.
03:15 Maya Chen: we'll share SOC2 docs and the security pack link after the call. for KMS we support customer-managed keys, we can outline key rotations in the SOW.
03:25 Rajiv Malhotra: sweet. back to traffic modeling  —  we need to simulate real sessions including retry patterns. do you have a harness?
03:33 Liam Patel: yes, we'll use a k6-based harness with a token simulator that mirrors your distributions. we can replay anonymized request logs if you provide them  —  that gives most realistic tail behavior.
03:45 Sofia Torres: we'll export 7 days of anonymized traces. one gotcha: our burst patterns are driven by batch reconciliation jobs at 2am UTC that spike qps for ~10 minutes, we want to ensure graceful degradation.
03:59 Liam Patel: noted. we'll include burst scenarios: steady-state QPS, peak short burst at 200-220 QPS, and extreme stress at 350 QPS for failover testing.
04:12 Rajiv Malhotra: what's your recommended concurrency per GPU for our model size? we are evaluating a 13B open model quantized to int8.
04:22 Liam Patel: for a 13B int8 on T4-class or equivalent, typical concurrency to keep latency sub-1s is 6-10 tokens-per-step concurrency, but actual numbers depend on sequence length. we'll include kernel selection and batching in the run. note that quantization gives cost improvements but watch p99 tail.
04:41 Maya Chen: to be concrete, we'll propose a benchmark matrix:
- Scenario A: baseline steady 60 QPS with distribution you gave (70/25/5), measure p50/p95/p99 and tokens per second
- Scenario B: peak 200 QPS sustained 5 minutes, measure throughput and error rates
- Scenario C: burst 350 QPS short spike for 10 minutes to validate fallbacks and routing
- Scenario D: embedding-heavy burst (indexing) test at 400 QPS for embedding endpoint

04:58 Sofia Torres: that looks good. timeline wise how long for setup and runs?
05:03 Maya Chen: typical 1 week to onboard (keys, VPC peering if applicable), 1 week to instrument harness and ingest sample traces, then 1 week for the main benchmark runs and analysis, plus 1 week buffer for remediation  —  total 4 weeks.
05:16 Rajiv Malhotra: that fits our schedule. what metrics will you share post-run?
05:21 Liam Patel: we'll provide a benchmark report with p50/p95/p99 for latencies, throughput curves, error rates, tokenized cost estimate (per 1M tokens), and recommendation for batching/kv-cache settings and quantization profile.
05:32 Ethan Cole: can you also include model fallback plans and how we would route to hosted if dedicated is saturated? we need SLA coverage.
05:38 Maya Chen: yes, we'll include routing policy options (priority by latency or cost, region fallback), and typical failover behaviors. Dedicated pilot can be SLA-blessed with SLOs in SOW.
05:47 Sofia Torres: one more question on evaluation: for quality regression, we will run an eval set of ~500 prompts. how do you surface diffs?
05:54 Liam Patel: we'll run side-by-side outputs and diff metrics (exact match, BLEU-ish scores or embed-based similarity), plus human spot checks for critical flows. we'll flag any major regressions at the example/prompt level.
06:06 Rajiv Malhotra: ok perfect. anything else on cost modeling?
06:09 Maya Chen: we'll estimate unit token cost for each scenario and provide recommendations  —  e.g., batching, cache TTLs, and quantization to hit your 20% cost reduction target. often the biggest wins are KV caching for session prefix reuse and smart batching for throughput.
06:24 Maya Chen: recap of next steps: we'll send benchmark plan and security pack by end of week, liam will prep harness, nexus to provide traces and prompts, and we schedule benchmark run week of sep 6.
06:36 Sofia Torres: sounds good, thanks everyone.
06:39 Maya Chen: thanks  —  we'll follow up via email with links and the SOW draft. bye.

Notes about transcription: minor transcription noise e.g., "K-V cash" instead of "KV cache", occasional speaker label switched early but context preserved.
notes: Customer provided baseline: peak ~180 QPS, sustained 60 QPS, concurrency ~80
Token distribution proposed: 70% short, 25% medium, 5% long
Embeddings ~10% of traffic with burst indexing windows
Success criteria: p95/p99 latency targets, >=20% unit cost reduction, no major quality regressions on eval set
